title: A soda for people who did not believe in soda commercials
lede: OK Soda is remembered for its cans, its hotline and its manifesto. It is rarely remembered for how it tasted, which is most of the explanation for what happened to it.

chapters.title: The second-best-known word in the world
chapters.cap: the age range Coca-Cola said the drink was aimed at, “particularly young men”
chapters.body:
Sergio Zyman had been senior vice president of marketing for Coca-Cola USA until 1986. After seven years as a consultant he came back in August 1993 as the company’s chief marketing officer.[^1] The essayist Michael Schulman later described the rehiring as a surprise, since Zyman’s “last brainstorm” had been [New Coke](/new-coke/).[^13]

Coca-Cola said its understanding of teenagers rested on years of study, including a two-year “Global Teenager” program that employed graduate students from MIT, and on a year of field research for this product. The research described a generation with, in Time’s paraphrase, “an acute sense of diminished expectations.”[^6] The company also had a gap to fill: Pepsi’s Mountain Dew held 3.5% of the US soft drink market, and Coca-Cola’s citrus brand Mello Yello held 0.3%.[^6]

The name came from a claim Coca-Cola repeated to reporters: that O.K. is the most widely recognized expression in the world, and Coca-Cola the second.[^6][^7][^8] The company already owned the word for soft drinks: a US trademark registration for OK, issued in 1978, is listed in the Patent and Trademark Office’s records under Coca-Cola’s name, and the 1994 application claimed it.[^12][^11]

pull.text: It underpromises. It doesn’t say, ‘This is the next great thing.’
pull.who: Brian Lanahan, manager of special projects, Coca-Cola marketing, in Time, May 30, 1994[^6]

chapters.artCaption: The cans were black, gray and red, with deadpan faces. Time compared them to post-office wanted pictures.[^6] Original illustration, not the real artwork.

chapters.title: Four cans, because the focus groups could not pick one
chapters.cap: can designs shown to focus groups before Coca-Cola decided to use four
chapters.body:
Coca-Cola introduced OK at a news conference in New York on April 20, 1994. The New York Times called it “a cola-colored, full-calorie soda” and a gambit against the independent brands in “the growing market for alternative beverages.” The company said the taste defied categorization. Reporters who tried it detected “a slight orange or citrus flavor.”[^4] The agency was Wieden & Kennedy of Portland, Oregon, known for its Nike advertising.[^4]

Five days later Advertising Age reported that Coca-Cola, “in its rush to develop new products,” would within 30 days bring to market “a new brand that’s admittedly not fully formed.”[^5] The trademark record gives May 6, 1994 as the date of first use in commerce.[^11]

By late May the drink was on sale in what Time counted as nine cities “from Boston to Seattle.” NPR named Austin, Denver, Minneapolis–St. Paul and Seattle.[^6][^7] There were four can designs, chosen after focus groups failed to agree on one out of more than 50. The artwork came from alternative cartoonists, among them Daniel Clowes and Charles Burns.[^6][^8] Time reported that Coca-Cola planned to roll the drink out across the United States that summer and take it abroad by the end of the year.[^6]

image.caption: The four original can designs, photographed in 2006. Photo: TeemPlayer, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.[^21]
image.alt: Four gray and silver OK Soda cans side by side, each with a red-bordered OK box and black line drawings of faces

chapters.title: 1-800-I-FEEL-OK
chapters.cap: calls to the hotline by September 1994, according to Coca-Cola
chapters.body:
The advertising did not show anyone drinking anything. It began with chain letters, mailed in the test markets about two weeks before the television and print ads, telling recipients to show the letter “to six close friends.”[^6] Cans and posters carried numbered “coincidences,” short tales about people who had or had not drunk OK, and lines from a ten-point manifesto.[^8][^13]

The center of it was a toll-free number. Callers could hear recorded messages, take a true-or-false “OK Personality Inventory,” or leave a message of their own. Time reported that Coca-Cola had paid its agency to plant a hostile one, from a “Pam H.” who resented being told that everything would be O.K.[^6] Real callers were less scripted. One said: “this stuff tastes like crap.”[^6] Another called it “carbonated tree sap,” and the agency put the phrase in the ads.[^8]

By early September Coca-Cola said the line had taken more than a million calls, from a product sold in a handful of cities.[^8] Mark Pendergrast, as quoted in The Believer, wrote that kids called “just to see what happened.”[^13]

pull.text: The most important thing is advertising.
pull.who: Tom Pirko, president of Bevmark, on what makes people choose a soft drink, NPR’s All Things Considered, May 27, 1994[^7]

chapters.title: “The first one tastes good, but you don’t want a second”
chapters.cap: 12-packs a week, at most, sold by a nine-store Twin Cities supermarket chain
chapters.body:
Coca-Cola told Time the flavor came from the observation that teenagers drink everything from colas to lemon-lime, so it blended those tastes into one reddish-brown soda.[^6] On NPR a consultant who had worked for both Coke and Pepsi described it as “a little bit like going to a fountain and mixing a little bit of Coke with a little root beer and Dr. Pepper and maybe throwing in some orange.”[^7]

In Minneapolis, The Washington Post found that drinkers had reached the same comparison on their own. Each of the first four people the reporter interviewed said it tasted like a “suicide,” the mix you get by pressing every button on a self-serve dispenser.[^8] In a focus group there in May, the 15-to-17-year-olds “eventually warmed up” to it and the 18-to-20-year-olds “never warmed up at all.” Both groups loved the 800 number.[^6]

By the start of September the Post reported “dismal sales” in the Twin Cities. One store clerk said Coke’s distributor had pulled the product from the shelves. The manager of another store said he had not sold a single 12-pack. Coca-Cola declined to comment on sales, and the hotline told callers its services were paused until September 12 “for purely arbitrary reasons.”[^8]

pull.text: We sell at most 10 12-packs a week, maybe, and 20 liter bottles, which is our most popular size. Overall, I’d say it’s not doing great.
pull.who: Paul Ruhme, grocery manager of Byerly’s, The Washington Post, Sep 3, 1994[^8]

chapters.artCaption: Drinkers in Minneapolis independently compared the taste to every fountain flavor in one cup.[^8] Original illustration.

chapters.title: “Not the type of profitable volume we needed”
chapters.cap: cases sold, a little more, before the phase-out
chapters.body:
The national rollout that Time had described for the summer of 1994 did not happen, and neither, as far as we could find, did the launch in four other countries that Coca-Cola had announced.[^6][^8] The company’s annual report on Form 10-K for 1994 lists “OK soda” once, between caffeine free TAB and Fresca, in a sentence naming its soft drink products. It says nothing else about it.[^1]

On September 13, 1995 The New York Times carried a four-sentence item from Atlanta under the headline “Phasing Out a Soda.” A spokesman, Randy Donaldson, said Coca-Cola had sold more than one million cases since the drink’s introduction and that this was not enough.[^9] The next 10-K’s product list does not include it.[^3]

Coca-Cola spent $1,308 million on advertising in 1994, up from $1,126 million the year before.[^1] What share of that went to OK was never disclosed.

pull.text: We just didn’t generate the type of profitable volume we needed with OK, so we decided not to continue it in those test markets.
pull.who: Randy Donaldson, Coca-Cola spokesman, The New York Times, Sep 13, 1995[^9]

chapters.title: The product died. The brand lived on.
chapters.cap: the year the US trademark registration was canceled
chapters.body:
The trademark outlasted the drink on paper. Coca-Cola’s application for the red-boxed OK mark was still pending when the phase-out was announced. It was registered in March 1997 and canceled in December 2003 for want of a declaration of continued use.[^11]

In 1997 Time used OK as its example of how marketers had misread Generation X: “The nine-city campaign fizzled.”[^10] The cartoonist Daniel Clowes said in 2010 that the eyes on his can were Charles Manson’s, and that there was by then “a whole cult devoted to OK.”[^14] In 2014 The Believer found old poster art selling for hundreds of dollars on eBay, and asked Peter Wegner, who wrote the manifesto, what had gone wrong.[^13]

His answer was short: people did not want to consume the drink, and very much wanted to consume the brand.[^13] We found no revival of either.

pull.text: So the product died. The brand lived on.
pull.who: Peter Wegner, associate creative director on the campaign, in The Believer, Feb 2014[^13]
